Admissions
Admissions is an annual process, with an application deadline of December 15. All applications are submitted online. The traits of the best applicants are superlative training in physics, a strong work ethic, substantial research experience in the physical sciences, evidence of independence and creativity, maturity of purpose, and good communication ability.
The elements of the application are:
Statement of purpose (research interests and experience, career plans), written in English, and not to exceed 1,000 words
Academic transcript
Separate listing of physics and astronomy courses (in a more standardized format)
Curriculum vitae
Three letters of recommendation
Passing English language proficiency scores from TOEFL, IELTS, or DET (for non-native English speakers)
Application fee (or a request for a fee waiver — see below)
(Optional) Essay conveying any relevant information not represented elsewhere in the application, such as personal experiences
(Optional) General and Physics GRE scores
(Optional) Other supporting materials, such as papers in progress
Please note:
There are no "cut-offs" on grades, GRE scores, etc.
All applications will be read completely and carefully.
Application fee waivers:
We do not want the application fee to be a significant barrier to applying. The Graduate School accepts requests for fee waivers from applicants with financial hardship, or from applicants who have attended certain recruiting events.
The Horizon Fellowship:
Applicants to our Ph.D. program may also indicate their interest in being considered for a Horizon Fellowship. This fellowship is intended for students showing exceptional promise who would benefit from an additional year of training to strengthen their academic or research preparation. It provides an additional (sixth) year of guaranteed financial support. Among the reasons an applicant might want to be considered for a Horizon Fellowship are:
There were limited opportunities for research or rigorous physics courses at their undergraduate institution.
They come from a physics background and would benefit from extra time to study astronomy (or vice versa).
They have been out of academia for a while and would benefit from extra time to re-adjust to the academic environment.
Incoming Horizon Fellows work with faculty members to design a customized one-year academic plan, which may involve taking courses or developing research skills. They are fully integrated into our graduate student community from the moment they arrive, and are also invited to participate in the Graduate Scholars Program, a cohort-based peer-to-peer mentoring program.
Applicants who opt to be considered for the Horizon Fellowship program will also be considered for regular admission; indicating interest in this program does not decrease the chance of being chosen for regular admission.
Please direct administrative-related questions to Polly Strauss, Academic Program Administrator (pstrauss@princeton.edu).
